rules.law_name: New Jersey Anti-Eviction Act / Eviction Law
rules.title: Statutory grounds and notices for eviction
rules.requirement: A landlord may file for eviction only under specified statutory grounds, including certain conversion or owner-occupancy situations, termination of employment-based housing, or listed drug, assault, theft, human-trafficking, and related civil-liability grounds. Required Notices to Quit vary by ground, and misuse of certain owner-occupancy or removal-from-use notices can lead to treble damages and fees.
rules.key_value: Notice periods include 3 days, 2 months, and 3 years depending on the ground; up to five one-year stays in certain conversion cases; treble damages plus attorney fees/costs for specified violations

coverage.other_unresolvable: The excerpted grounds apply to specific situations such as condominium/cooperative/fee-simple conversion, employment-conditioned tenancies, and specified criminal or civil-liability conduct; broader Eviction Law coverage is not fully stated in this part.
coverage.summary: The excerpt covers residential eviction grounds and protections under New Jersey’s Eviction Law for specified conversion, employment, and misconduct situations.

rules.exemptions: No action may be brought against a senior citizen tenant or disabled tenant with protected tenancy status while that status or protected period remains in effect; several grounds also require that the lease expire before suit, and some offense-based grounds have two-year filing limits.
rules.penalty: If a tenant vacates after an owner-occupancy notice and the landlord does not occupy for at least six months, or if property removed from residential use is used residentially within five years, the landlord may be liable for three times damages plus attorney fees and costs; removal-from-use violations may also carry a civil penalty up to $10,000 per violation.
rules.interaction: The document also states that rooming and boarding houses, public housing, foreclosure situations, and protected-tenancy laws interact with or add to the Eviction Law’s protections.
rules.quoted_span: The landlord may file for eviction, if the owner of a building or mobile home park, which is constructed as or being converted to a condominium, cooperative or fee simple ownership, seeks to evict a tenant or sublessee whose initial tenancy began after the master deed

rules.law_name: Owner-Occupied Two- and Three-Family Dwelling Eviction Notice Rule
rules.title: Evictions from landlord-occupied two- and three-family dwellings
rules.requirement: Tenants in landlord-occupied two- and three-family dwellings can be removed only by court order and only if the landlord proves one of the listed grounds, such as lease expiration, nonpayment, disorderly conduct, damage, repeated rule violations, or lease violations with a reserved right of re-entry. The landlord must give the applicable Notice to Quit except that no further notice is required before court action for nonpayment of rent.
rules.key_value: 3 months for at-will or year-to-year tenancy; 1 month for month-to-month and other tenancies; 3 days for disorderly, destructive, written-rule, or lease-violation grounds

coverage.small_owner_exception: Applies specifically when the landlord occupies a two- or three-family dwelling.
coverage.other_unresolvable: Whether the landlord occupies the property and the tenancy type determine the notice period.
coverage.summary: Applies to tenants living in landlord-occupied two- and three-family dwellings.

rules.exemptions: No further notice is required before bringing an eviction action when the tenant stays after failing to pay rent.
rules.interaction: This section provides special eviction grounds and notice periods for owner-occupied two- and three-family dwellings apart from the general Eviction Law grounds summarized elsewhere in the document.
rules.quoted_span: Tenants of landlord-occupied two- and three-family dwellings can be removed only when a court issues an order for eviction. However, in these cases, the landlord must prove that the tenant

rules.law_name: Regulations Governing Rooming and Boarding Houses
rules.title: Rooming and boarding house eviction good-cause and notice requirements
rules.requirement: Rooming and boarding house owners must follow the Eviction Law’s good-cause and notice requirements when evicting residents, unless the Bureau orders otherwise. The owner must also give the County Welfare Board at least three working days’ notice before starting an eviction action for any resident.
rules.key_value: At least 3 working days’ notice to the County Welfare Board

coverage.other_unresolvable: The building must have living units occupied by unrelated persons without private kitchens and bathrooms, unless an exception in the Rooming and Boarding House Act applies.
coverage.summary: Applies to rooming or boarding houses, generally buildings with at least two living units occupied by unrelated persons without private kitchens and bathrooms.

rules.exemptions: Exceptions include hotels with more than 85 percent temporary occupancy by people with homes elsewhere, school and college dormitories, buildings housing only college students, and certain residences for the disabled.
rules.interaction: The rule incorporates the New Jersey Eviction Law’s good-cause and notice requirements for rooming and boarding house residents, unless otherwise ordered by the Bureau.
rules.quoted_span: require owners of rooming and boarding houses to follow the good causes and notice requirements of the Eviction Law when evicting residents, except if otherwise ordered by the Bureau (N.J.A.C. 5:27-3.3(c)).

rules.title: Tenant protections after foreclosure
rules.requirement: Foreclosure alone is not a ground to evict a residential tenant in New Jersey. A new owner who bought a foreclosed property must give required notices, and a buyer who wants to personally occupy the home as a primary residence must give a 90-day Notice to Quit and may not evict before an existing lease expires.
rules.key_value: 90-day Notice to Quit for buyer personal occupancy after foreclosure; new owner notice within 10 business days after sale

coverage.other_unresolvable: Applies when a person acquires a foreclosed property containing residential rental units; notice method varies depending on whether the property has 10 or fewer dwelling units or more than 10 dwelling units.
coverage.summary: Applies to tenants in residential rental properties affected by foreclosure.

rules.exemptions: Month-to-month tenants and two- and three-family owner-occupied units are not exempt from the 90-day notice requirements.
rules.penalty: The document identifies prohibited pressure tactics in connection with monetary offers to vacate but does not state a specific penalty in this excerpt.
rules.interaction: The document states that federal foreclosure protections do not preempt any State or local law providing longer time periods or additional tenant protections.
rules.quoted_span: Foreclosure alone is not grounds for eviction in New Jersey. In Chase Manhattan Bank v. Josephson, 135 N.J. 209 (1994) the court held that when a lender or other buyer takes possession of the property, the residential tenant comes with the property.

rules.title: Protection against retaliatory eviction or nonrenewal
rules.requirement: A landlord may not retaliate against a tenant by eviction, substantially changing lease terms, or refusing to renew because the tenant exercised protected rights. Protected conduct includes enforcing lease or legal rights, making good-faith health or safety complaints after notice to the landlord and time to cure, organizing or joining a tenant organization, or refusing retaliatory lease changes.

coverage.small_owner_exception: Owner-occupied two- or three-family dwellings are excluded from the reprisal law described in the document.
coverage.summary: Applies to all rental properties used for dwelling purposes, including mobile homes, except owner-occupied two- or three-family dwellings.

rules.exemptions: Owner-occupied two- or three-family dwellings are exempt.
rules.penalty: If a landlord takes reprisal action, the tenant may sue the landlord for damages in a civil action.
rules.interaction: This anti-reprisal protection operates alongside state and local tenant rights that tenants may attempt to enforce without retaliation.
rules.quoted_span: A landlord cannot take reprisal action against a tenant by eviction, substantial alteration of a lease or its terms, or refusal to renew a lease when a tenant exercises certain civil rights (N.J.S.A. 2A:42-10.10).

rules.law_name: Senior Citizens and Disabled Protected Tenancy Act
rules.title: Protected tenancy for seniors and disabled tenants in condominium or cooperative conversion
rules.requirement: Eligible senior citizens, permanently disabled tenants, and certain disabled veterans in a building being converted to condominium, cooperative, or fee-simple ownership may be protected from eviction for 40 years. To qualify, tenants must meet age, disability or veteran-disability criteria, have lived in the building at least one year before the conversion recording date, and satisfy the stated income limit.
rules.key_value: Protected from eviction for 40 years; income not more than 3 times average county per-person income or $50,000, whichever is greater; applications generally within 60 days

coverage.other_unresolvable: Applies to qualifying tenants in buildings being converted to condominium, cooperative, or fee simple ownership of units; eligibility depends on age, disability or veteran status, income, residence duration, and application process.
coverage.summary: Applies to qualifying senior, disabled, and certain disabled veteran tenants in buildings undergoing condominium, cooperative, or fee-simple conversion.

rules.exemptions: Protected status can end if the agency terminates it or the protected tenancy period expires; the document also states that applications generally must be filed within 60 days, although late filings may be accepted for good reason if conversion has not yet taken place.
rules.interaction: The document notes that tenants in Hudson County may be eligible for additional protected tenancy under the Tenant Protection Act of 1992.
rules.quoted_span: Tenants may be protected from eviction for 40 years if their family income is not more than three (3) times the average per person income in their county or $50,000.00, whichever  is greater (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.28).
rules.conflict_note: The document heading refers to the “Senior Citizens and Disabled Protected Tenancy Act,” but one passage describes protected tenancy status pursuant to the “Senior Citizens and Disabled Protected Tenancy Act of 1992,” while another cites the “Senior Citizens and Disabled Protected Tenancy Act of 1981.”

rules.title: Additional protected tenancy in qualified counties
rules.requirement: The Tenant Protection Law of 1992 extends conversion-related protected-tenancy protections to qualified tenants in qualified counties who were not eligible as senior citizens or disabled persons under the Senior Citizens and Disabled Protected Tenancy Act. The document states that, at present, Hudson County is the only qualified county.
rules.key_value: Applies in qualified counties; document states the only qualified county is Hudson County

coverage.other_unresolvable: Coverage depends on being a qualified tenant in a qualified county and living in a building converted or being converted; the document states that the only qualified county at present is Hudson County.
coverage.summary: Applies to qualified tenants in qualified counties in buildings converted or being converted, currently described as Hudson County only.

rules.exemptions: Tenants who were eligible for protected tenancy as senior citizens or disabled persons under the Senior Citizens and Disabled Protected Tenancy Act are not the target of this extension.
rules.interaction: This law adds protected-tenancy coverage for certain conversion tenants who are not covered by the Senior Citizens and Disabled Protected Tenancy Act.
rules.quoted_span: The Tenant Protection Law of 1992 amendment extends protections to qualified tenants in qualified counties in buildings converted or being converted who were not eligible for Protected Tenancy as either Senior Citizens or Disabled Persons under the “Senior Citizens and Disabled Protected Tenancy Act of 1981” (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.40 to -61.59; N.J.A.C. 5:24-3.1 to -3.4).
